newsitem.title: JAPAN: Matsushita returns to basics in profit recovery.
newsitem.headline: Matsushita returns to basics in profit recovery.

text.p: Humiliated by Hollywood, zapped by the videogame market, Japan's Matsushita Electric had to go back to basics to boost its profits in the first quarter of this business year.

Matsushita Electric Industrial Co on Tuesday reported a group net profit of 18.5 billion yen ($172 million) in the first quarter that ended on June 30, a sharp turnaround from a 151.3 billion yen ($1.41 billion) loss a year before.

The giant consumer electronics firm said that net profits actually jumped 44 percent in the April-June quarter from the same quarter in 1995. Matsushita said that if not for the sale of an 80 percent share in U.S. film maker MCA Inc, it would have turned a 12.9 billion yen ($120 million) profit in the first quarter of 1995.

While the weak yen accounted for the bulk of the profit increase, analysts said the strong showing in the first quarter indicates success in its strategy to focus more on its stable hardware business.
A drop in the yen makes Japanese companies more competitive overseas, because this lowers the price of their goods in foreign exchange terms.
"Matsushita's decision to give up management control in MCA was so far, so good," said Katsuhiko Sugiyama, president of think tank Musashi Development Co.
"Matsushita, and Sony too, are eventually reaping profits from their existing businesses."

Overall, Matsushita said its group first-quarter sales rose a healthy 13 percent to 1.72 trillion yen ($16.0 billion) over the year-earlier period. Operating profits soared 50 percent to 44.4 billion yen ($414 million) as higher sales and the weak yen more than offset losses due to declines in product prices.

Domestic sales of information-related equipment, such as cellular phones, and consumer electronics, which have been depressed for several years, accounted for much of Matsushita's surprisingly strong profit gains, a Matsushita spokesman said.
"Sales declines were recorded only in semiconductors and the software business at our affiliates, such as Victor Co of Japan," said the spokesman.

Booming sales of consumer electronics, which reflect strong housing starts and a planned rise in the consumption tax next year, also helped Matsushita, which overwhelms its rivals in the number of products it sells.
Industry analysts expect domestic shipments of refrigerators, air conditioners, televisions and washing machines to climb to record highs in calendar 1996.

When Matsushita sold its majority stake in MCA last year after management trouble, some analysts said the loss of the film-making unit would hurt Matsushita's growth potential, which depends highly on the saturated consumer electronics market.

Matsushita was also nudged out of the booming videogame market by rivals Sony Corp and Sega Entertainment Ltd. Sales of Matsushita's 3DO videogame players fell short of its target due to a lack of attractive software.
Goldman Sachs (Japan) analyst Hitoshi Kuriyama said the sale of MCA shares clarified the course the company has chosen to take for the medium term.

"The company has decided to focus more on the hardware business, namely value-added parts," he said. "Matsushita is trying to maximize profits from key devices and other hardware businesses in the mid-term, and the good first-quarter results reflect that strategy to a certain extent."
